preamble: Debuccalization of the flap [ɾ] to a glottal stop [ʔ]. The clearest case is the Satsugū (Kagoshima) dialect of Japanese. There, a final high vowel is dropped and the consonant left in coda position becomes the moraic obstruent /Q/, which is realized as [ʔ] at the end of an utterance and before nasals, vowels and glides. In Kagoshima city and parts of southern Satsuma this also applies to the flap of the verb ending -ru, so kuru 'to come' becomes [kuʔ], the same as kutsu 'shoes', kubi 'neck' and kuchi 'mouth'. In nouns the flap more often glides to [i] instead (tori > toi 'bird').

examples.from: Standard Japanese 来る kuru [kɯɾɯ] 'to come'
examples.note: In Kagoshima city and parts of Satsunan, the verb ending -ru undergoes the same reduction to /Q/ as final ki, ku, chi, tsu, bi, bu, so 'come' becomes homophonous with 'shoes', 'neck', 'mouth', 'nail' and 'comb'.

examples.from: Standard Japanese 知りません shirimasen [ɕiɾimasen] 'I don't know'
examples.note: Word-medially the reduced syllable is also /Q/, which is realized as a glottal stop before a nasal.

sources: Wikipedia (2026). 薩隅方言 (Satsugū dialect). https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/薩隅方言
